analysis.file_name: AI Is Creating Jobs... For People Who Already Have Jobs.pdf
analysis.title: AI Is Creating Jobs... For People Who Already Have Jobs
key_insights: A Stanford (Chandar) and King's College London (Klein Teeselink) paper covering 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records across 41 countries (Jan 2021 to Mar 2026) finds senior employment at AI adopters rose 6.7% relative to matched non-adopters, total employment rose 3.3%, and junior employment fell 2.5%.

The study compares 26,102 foreign affiliates of multinationals that began posting AI-related job ads after ChatGPT's launch with non-adopting affiliates in the same country and sector. Adoption is instrumented with AI adoption by other multinationals headquartered in the parent's home metro.

Junior share of employment at adopters ended 1.9 percentage points below controls by March 2026. Juniors held 57.1% of positions at baseline, so this is a 3.3% relative drop in their share. Junior employment fell 2.9% within a year of ChatGPT's launch and then stayed flat, while senior employment barely moved for 18 months and then rose steadily.

The junior employment decline on its own is not statistically significant. The 6.7% senior gain and the 1.9pp drop in junior share are significant. The article says Bloomberg rounded the junior decline up to 3%.
For the average treated affiliate (about 255 positions in October 2022, 145 junior), adoption meant about 8 more seniors and about 4 fewer juniors by March 2026.

The junior share fell in 23 of 31 countries with enough data. Seven declines are statistically significant: US, UK, Spain, Poland, Brazil, Mexico and Saudi Arabia. Losses are deeper in richer, more digitized economies and smaller where labor laws are more rigid.

In 21 of 22 occupation groups the change in employment share is under half a percentage point. Computer and mathematical jobs are the exception, with share up 0.8pp, yet their junior share fell 3.3pp. Significant junior-share declines: legal -4.9pp, computer and math -3.3pp, business and financial operations -3.2pp, sales -2.6pp, management -1.0pp.

A census paper cited in the article finds graduates of the most AI-exposed majors saw their odds of landing a job right after graduation fall 5 percentage points and starting pay fall about 13% since ChatGPT launched. Stanford Digital Economy Lab estimates employment among 22-to-25 year olds in highly AI-exposed jobs is 19% below the path of less-exposed roles, versus 13% in the August 2025 study.

Goldman's AI Adoption Tracker (Oct 1) describes labor impact as 'visible but narrow'. It cites drags in marketing, graphic design, customer service and some tech occupations, offset by data-center-exposed construction jobs up 317k since 2022. The correlation between AI adoption and labor market slack has strengthened recently.

Goldman's global analysis (August) finds a 10% AI exposure score is associated with a 0.1pp drag on annual headcount growth in France, Canada and the US, with negligible effects elsewhere. Effects are more visible for entry-level workers or high-displacement-risk occupations.

BofA's Global Economic Weekly (mid-August, 'SurvAIval of the fattest') sees little evidence of broad AI-related job destruction but says AI 'may already be weighing on employment growth in some industries and on entry-level hiring in particular'.
The article ties the findings to a low-hire, low-fire labor market: initial claims below 200K for a fourth straight week and September payrolls of 29K, below all estimates.

The authors caution the result is a firm-level relative gain, not an aggregate one. Their general-equilibrium model shows aggregate employment can fall even as adopters grow, because AI raises output while shrinking labor's share. The article also argues that cutting the junior bench hollows out the future senior workforce.

Goldman's tracker shows 23.8% of US firms using AI in regular business functions, with 27.6% expected within six months and nearly 50% in information, professional and finance sectors. Goldman sized eventual US displacement at roughly 15 million workers (June).

risk_factors: Junior hiring squeeze may broaden as AI adoption rises from about a quarter of firms toward half.

cross_bank_references: Goldman and BofA are described as on the same page: AI's labor impact is visible but narrow overall and concentrated at the entry level.

tension_points.bull_case: AI adopters grow and total headcount rises 3.3%, with senior employment up 6.7%, so AI is changing the mix of jobs within organisations rather than reducing overall employment (the paper and KCL press release framing).
tension_points.bear_case: The gains are firm-level, not economy-wide. Adopters may take share from non-adopters, and the paper's general-equilibrium model shows aggregate employment can fall. Junior hiring is shrinking, which hollows out the future senior workforce.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Adoption rising from about a quarter of US firms toward half, which the article expects to broaden the junior squeeze rather than fade.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI adopters are hiring seniors but cutting or not replacing juniors, and the squeeze is likely to broaden as adoption climbs.
theme_stances.evidence: AI is labor saving for junior workers and labor expanding for seniors
